1. Search by effect or technique.
The search bar keys off the effect or technique, so try a keyword like portrait, glass effect, animation, or match and move. You don't need the exact title, near enough usually surfaces it.

2. Use the filters to narrow down.
Filter by what a hack does, the Canva feature it uses, difficulty, or Free and Pro, so on free Canva you see only the hacks you can do today.

3. Browse without a target.
Scroll the hacks page with the filters off, past the ones you didn't come looking for. That's how you find techniques you'd never have thought to search for.

4. Don't just watch, recreate.
A hack sticks when you do it, not when you watch it. Open Canva alongside one and recreate the steps on your own design. Minutes spent designing in Canva beat an hour watching.

emails.name: Free Template Follow-up 1
emails.subject: Turn one template into a month of posts

swaps.html: What to change each week so it never looks like a repeat.

{% assign fn = person.firstName | strip %}{% assign up = fn | upcase %}Hi {% if fn == blank %}there{% elsif fn == up %}{{ fn | capitalize }}{% else %}{{ fn | slice: 0 | upcase }}{{ fn | slice: 1, 100 }}{% endif %},

Keep the layout. Rotate three things:

1. The shot. New photos or clips each week, and vary the kind of shot too. A close-up one week, a wide shot the next. Same template, different feel.

2. The colour. Give each week one of your brand colours as the main colour. Two or three colours across a month still read as one set.

3. The headline length. A three-word headline and a ten-word one make the same template look like two designs.

What stays fixed is what people recognise you by: the layout, the font, the rhythm. That's what makes a feed look designed rather than assembled.

All the best,
Joe

emails.name: Free Template Follow-up 2
emails.subject: How to spot a template worth keeping

swaps.html: Three quick tests. Most templates fail the first one.

{% assign fn = person.firstName | strip %}{% assign up = fn | upcase %}Hi {% if fn == blank %}there{% elsif fn == up %}{{ fn | capitalize }}{% else %}{{ fn | slice: 0 | upcase }}{{ fn | slice: 1, 100 }}{% endif %},

Most templates are made for the preview image. They look great until the first edit, when the font won't change everywhere and the photo won't crop.

Three tests show whether a template is worth keeping:

1. It survives your edits.

Swap the font, the photo and the main colour. If everything updates cleanly and nothing breaks, it was built to be used, not just shown.

2. It stretches to a month of posts.

A template that only works for one post is a one-off. A good one carries a post a week without looking repetitive.

3. It shows why it works.

Clear hierarchy, colours you can rotate, an obvious place for the eye to land. You come away knowing a little more about design, not just holding one finished post.

The template you got passes all three. So does every template in the Best of Hacks Templates Pack.

Take it easy,
Joe
